newsitem.title: USA: Belgium's Verplaetse sees core EMU growing rapidly.
newsitem.headline: Belgium's Verplaetse sees core EMU growing rapidly.

text.p: European monetary union is likely to start with a core group of about six countries, but will expand rapidly as other nations meet the entry criteria, Belgian central bank head Alfons Verplaetse said on Wednesday.

Verplaetse, in Washington for international meetings, said he strongly believed that Belgium would be one of the founder members of the single currency, even though Belgian public debt is running at twice the recommended level for EMU.
But Verplaetse made clear that Belgium's debt excess meant it had to be certain to meet the other entry criteria for monetary union to the letter.
"The question of three percent is a question of 'to be or not to be' (for Belgium), we realise that," Verplaetse told Reuters in an interview. "There is no leeway on this."
Countries that want to meld their currencies into the proposed euro from 1999 must meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, public debt and budget deficits.

The fiscal criteria in the Maastricht Treaty -- which specify ideal levels of no more than three percent deficits to gross domestic product and a 60 percent ratio for debt -- have proved the hardest for most countries to achieve.

Belgium is arguing that although its debt -- at 130 percent of GDP -- is way out of line, the fact that it has a concrete plan to reduce the level to 60 percent by 2015 should gain it some points in the Maastricht test.
Yet Verplaetse made clear that Belgium's stance was not that the Maastricht criteria should be softened to allow key countries into monetary union regardless at all costs.

Noting that the Treaty clearly specified that high debt levels only had to be moving steadily toward the 60 percent target to be acceptable, he said it was equally true that excesses on the three percent goal were only tolerable in exceptional circumstances.

Such an interpretation would tend to exclude countries such as Italy, which have little chance of hitting the 3.0 percent deficit mark in the 1997 crunch year, from being in monetary union in the first round in 1999.

Declining to comment directly on the likelihood of Italy joining EMU at the start, Verplaetse said he believed that even if it did not make the grade in 1997, the lira would join soon after the 1999 launch.

"I am sure that very fast Italy will be a part of EMU, if not from the first day," he said, adding that it and other countries that were not founder EMU countries could even join before European notes and coins are issued at end-2001.
"I would be very happy if Italy, Spain and Britain were willing and able to join in the first round," he said. "But we have to start regardless. There can be no delay."

Asked whether countries such as Italy, Britain and Finland may have already disqualified themselves from early EMU entry by leaving their currencies outside Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992, Verplaetse said he did not believe this alone would bar their entry to the euro.
The Maastricht Treaty calls for would-be EMU currencies to have been trading stably in Europe's ERM for at least two years before they can be deemed eligible for EMU.

Noting that it was up to Europe's heads of state to make this decision, Verplaetse said his personal view was that exchange rate stability coupled with a commitment to keep the nominal exchange rate stable would be sufficient.
